title: The Challenge for Aging Leaders and Thinkers
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that aging leaders and thinkers lose productivity not because creativity fades but because they take fewer shots on goal. It cites research that productivity, defined as significant contributions through innovative thinking, peaks in the first two decades of a career. The author attributes the midcareer decline to growing personal obligations and divided focus. Examples include composers, scientists, painters and designers whose best work comes early, and the fact that most innovative companies are founded by people under 30. The lesson offered is that younger people simply pursue more opportunities and take more chances. Late-career leaders are urged to keep a steady pace through discipline, routines, collaboration and persistence, since sustained willingness to act is what preserves output.
points: Productivity falls with age because people attempt fewer new ideas, not because creativity declines.
Midcareer obligations and divided focus explain the drop in output.
Young innovators succeed largely because they pursue more opportunities and take more chances.
Discipline, routines, collaboration and persistence can keep late-career productivity as strong as early-career output.
quotes: As leaders and thinkers age, they don’t lose their creativity as much as they lose their energy and desire to compete. Simply put, they do not take as many shots on goal.

Creativity is ageless, but productivity (defined as significant contributions through innovative thinking) peaks within the first two decades of professional life. A flurry of activity occurs early on in a career, followed by a gradual decrease in output.

That’s why composers write their best scores before the age of 50, scientists write most of their breakthrough papers in their 30s, painters produce their most treasured works in their 20s, and designers strike it big in their 20s. Not surprisingly, the majority of highly innovative companies that bring new products or services to the marketplace are founded by entrepreneurs under 30.

It's not that younger people are more creative or think with more zest. They simply pursue more opportunities and take more chances. The lesson for leaders and thinkers as they approach the back nine of their careers is to keep a steady pace.

Through discipline, rigorous routines, collaborations, and steadfast persistence, productivity can be as strong in the later years as it was in the early years. The key is to maintain a focus on how many opportunities and challenges they pursue. If the shots on goal don’t decrease, neither will the productivity.
The willingness to act is always a difference-maker. This is especially true later in a career. The willingness to keep producing has the biggest impact on productivity.
